input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-559: Seminar in Systems. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: This course examines current topics in Systems. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Distributed Systems cluster, the Architecture and Operating Systems cluster, the Security cluster, or some combination of these three clusters. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[mit-xv6-book]
The xv6 book explains processes, system calls, traps, page tables, scheduling, locking, file systems, devices, concurrency, and isolation in a small Unix-like kernel. A process combines an address space with execution state and operating-system resources. A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service. A trap records processor state so the kernel can handle a system call, exception, or interrupt. Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory with permission bits. The scheduler selects runnable processes and switches processor context. Locks protect invariants when concurrent execution can access shared state. The file system organizes persistent data through inodes, directories, and logged updates. Analysis distinguishes user mode, privileged kernel code, hardware translation, interrupt state, resource ownership, and synchronization invariants.

[riscv-unprivileged]
The RISC-V ISA defines programmer-visible instructions, registers, memory operations, control transfer, exceptions, and ordering behavior. Integer register x0 always reads as zero, while the remaining integer registers hold software-visible values. Load instructions transfer data from memory into registers. Store instructions transfer register data to memory. Branch and jump instructions change control flow. Exceptions report conditions that require a defined transfer of control. Memory-ordering rules constrain how memory operations may be observed. Architecture analysis preserves data dependencies, control dependencies, and architectural state.

Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Distributed Systems cluster, the Architecture and Operating Systems cluster, the Security cluster, or some combination of these three clusters. Contact Hours: Lecture 3

beats.claim: A process combines an address space with execution state and operating-system resources.
beats.example: A web server process maintains its own memory space, open file descriptors, and CPU scheduling context.
beats.title: Process Definition and State
beats.visualDirection: Display a diagram showing a process boundary with labeled address space, execution state, and OS resource handles.

beats.claim: A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service.
beats.example: A process invokes a read system call to request data from a file, transitioning to kernel mode.
beats.title: System Call Mechanism
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart of control transfer between user space and kernel space with a labeled system call instruction.

beats.claim: A trap records processor state so the kernel can handle a system call, exception, or interrupt.
beats.example: When a process triggers a page fault, the CPU traps the fault, saves registers, and transfers to the kernel handler.
beats.title: Trap Handling and Context Switching
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a trap sequence with a processor state snapshot, kernel handler entry, and restored state return.

beats.claim: Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory with permission bits.
beats.example: A page table entry translates a virtual address to a physical frame while enforcing read/write/execute permissions.
beats.title: Virtual Memory Mapping
beats.visualDirection: Render a page table structure with virtual address bits, physical address bits, and permission flags.

beats.claim: The scheduler selects runnable processes and switches processor context.
beats.example: A round-robin scheduler picks the next process from the ready queue and saves the current context.
beats.title: Process Scheduling
beats.visualDirection: Draw a scheduler loop showing ready queue, context save/restore, and CPU allocation.

beats.claim: Locks protect invariants when concurrent execution can access shared state.
beats.example: A mutex lock prevents two processes from modifying a shared counter simultaneously.
beats.title: Concurrency and Locking
beats.visualDirection: Show a lock acquisition/release sequence with a shared variable and protected critical section.

beats.claim: The file system organizes persistent data through inodes, directories, and logged updates.
beats.example: An inode stores metadata for a file while directory entries link names to inode references.
beats.title: File System Organization
beats.visualDirection: Display a file system tree with inode blocks, directory entries, and journal log entries.

beats.claim: The RISC-V ISA defines programmer-visible instructions, registers, memory operations, control transfer, exceptions, and ordering behavior.
beats.example: Integer register x0 always reads as zero, while other registers hold software-visible values.
beats.title: RISC-V Instruction Set Basics
beats.visualDirection: List RISC-V register file with x0 marked as zero and other registers showing software values.

beats.claim: Memory-ordering rules constrain how memory operations may be observed.
beats.example: Store buffers ensure that writes are visible to other cores in a defined architectural order.
beats.title: Memory Ordering and Dependencies
beats.visualDirection: Show a memory operation sequence with ordering constraints and dependency arrows.

beats.claim: Analysis distinguishes user mode, privileged kernel code, hardware translation, interrupt state, resource ownership, and synchronization invariants.
beats.example: A security audit checks for proper privilege separation and lock invariants in a kernel module.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Provide a checklist template with checkboxes for each analysis category.

learningObjectives: Define the core abstraction layers that separate user applications from hardware execution.
Identify the fundamental components of a Unix-like kernel that manage system resources.
Recognize how abstraction enables modular design and security isolation in operating systems.
json.title: Foundations of System Abstraction
